phonemes.desc: Alveolar trill or tap [r], the first consonant of the solar god's name
Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ], the ayin that closes the Egyptian root rꜥ
Short open vowel [a], supplied by convention; Egyptian writing gave only rꜥ

pronunciation.approximation: 'rah-ʿA' — a rolled or tapped 'r', then a deep throaty 'ah' like the Arabic ع.

pronunciation.note: Rꜥ is a Tier-1 restoration. Egyptologists vocalise the name as Ra or Rꜥa, but the hieroglyphs record only rꜥ. The ayin (ꜥ) is the defining non-English sound — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses; the acute variant Rá is a modern stress marker, not an ancient vowel sign.

domains.title: Sun, Creation, Kingship
domains.subtitle: The domain of Rꜥ
domains.lead: Rꜥ is the sun as sovereignty: creator of the ordered world each dawn, father of the king who rules in his name, and nightly conqueror of the serpent of chaos. Egyptian theology unfolded him in three acts — Khepri the scarab at dawn, Rꜥ reigning at noon, Atum the aged creator at dusk — one god in three phases.

cards.name: Solar Barque
cards.desc: Ra sails the Mandjet by day and the Mesektet through the underworld, defeating Apophis each night (Book of the Dead, spell 15).

cards.name: Khepri, Ra, Atum
cards.desc: He is the scarab at dawn, the reigning sun at noon, and the weary creator at evening — one solar life in three bodies.

cards.name: Eye of Ra
cards.desc: His eye, embodied as Sekhmet or Hathor, punishes rebellion and returns as the protective uraeus on his brow (Book of the Heavenly Cow).

cards.name: Kingship
cards.desc: The pharaoh rules as Ra's son — the royal titulary names him heir of Ra — and every obelisk is a frozen ray of the sun-god's first light.

mythology.lead: Rꜥ's theology is Egypt's most complete vision of order (maat): the sun's daily circuit is a voyage, a kingship and a war. Each dawn the god is born in the east; each night he dies and must be defended; every royal tomb and solar temple re-stages that victory on earth.

myths.title: The Barque of Millions of Years
myths.text: The central image of Rꜥ theology is the barque called Mandjet, 'Boat of Millions of Years', in which the god sails the sky by day, and the Mesektet, in which he crosses the underworld by night. The underworld books — the Amduat and the Book of Gates — map the twelve hours of darkness: at each gate Rꜥ must pass guardians, recite their names, and survive the waiting ambush of Apopis, the serpent of chaos who rises from the primordial waters to swallow the sun. Other gods row; the souls of the justified dead join his crew; and at the twelfth hour the scarab Khepri rolls the renewed sun up from the eastern horizon (Book of the Dead, spell 15; Book of Gates). The theology makes every sunrise a contested event: light is not a fact but a nightly victory, re-won while humanity sleeps.

myths.title: The Distant Goddess and the First Men
myths.text: In the myth called 'The Destruction of Mankind', preserved in royal tombs of the Nineteenth–Twentieth Dynasties and on the gilded shrine of Tutankhamun (the 'Book of the Heavenly Cow'), humankind plots rebellion against Rꜥ — who, he says, has grown old, 'his bones silver, his flesh gold, his hair true lapis'. He sends his Eye against them as a raging lioness, the goddess Sekhmet, who slaughters until the gods fear nothing human will survive. Rꜥ halts her by stratagem: seven thousand jars of beer are dyed red with ochre and flooded across the field; Sekhmet drinks, believing it blood, and wakes gentle as Hathor — the returning Eye that becomes the uraeus coiled on the king's brow. The myth is a theology of measured wrath: the same solar power that nearly annihilates the world is tricked into mercy and worn thereafter as protection. Divine anger, Egyptian theology insists, must be outwitted into becoming grace.

myths.title: The Secret Name of Ra
myths.text: Rꜥ ruled by a hidden name — in Egyptian belief the seat of a god's power. Isis, 'a woman excellent of counsel', fashioned a serpent from the god's own spittle fallen to the earth and set it to bite him. No physic of any god could ease the agony, for the wound was made of Rꜥ's own essence. Isis alone could heal him — and would not, until he told her his true name. Rꜥ offered titles one by one: 'I am Khepri at dawn, Rꜥ at noon...' But Isis held out for the hidden name, and in the end the great god whispered it into her bosom and withdrew it from her, 'so that she passed it on to her son Horus' — and thereby, the tale adds, she became mistress of the gods (Leiden Papyrus J 395, c. 1200 BCE). The myth concedes the limits of solar omnipotence: even the sun is subject to time, venom and the older magic of a goddess — and sovereignty, it turns out, is finally something that can be told.

myths.title: Nut and the Five Days Outside the Year
myths.text: Rꜥ once cursed the sky-goddess Nut so that she could bear no child 'in any year, on any day' — jealousy of the generations she would mother. Nut wept to Thoth, lord of the moon's reckonings, who played draughts with the moon-goddess and won a seventy-second part of her light — enough to make five new days, which lie outside the 360-day year. On these epagomenal days Nut bore five children: Osiris, Horus the Elder, Seth, Isis and Nephthys — the generation whose feud fills the whole of Egyptian myth (Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride 12; the tale also stands behind the Cairo Calendar). The story turns calendrical necessity into cosmogony: the five days outside time are exactly where the drama of time's rulers could begin, and Rꜥ's jealous prohibition becomes the loophole through which salvation enters the world.

myths.title: The King's Ascension
myths.text: The Old Kingdom Pyramid Texts, cut inside the tombs of kings from Unas onward, turn Rꜥ's voyage into the king's itinerary: 'You shall ascend to the sky... you shall stand upon the smoke-cloud... you shall go up to where your father is.' The dead king is bathed, robed and ferried to join Rꜥ's crew — 'rower of Rꜥ, ferryman of the god who is in the sky' — while spells make him Rꜥ's son and other, darker hymns boast he will assimilate the gods' powers to himself (Pyramid Texts, Unas and Teti pyramids; Faulkner's translation). Solar eschatology begins here: heaven is not a place but a posting, a seat in the barque of millions earned by the office of kingship. Egypt's entire political theology flows from the metaphor — to rule is to crew the sun — and three thousand years of pharaonic titulary never abandoned it.

lore.syncretism: Rꜥ absorbed and was absorbed. At Heliopolis he fused with Atum, 'the All', and with the scarab Khepri; in the New Kingdom the Theban god Amun merged with him into Amun-Rꜥ, 'king of the gods', the composite patron of empire whose priests would one day rival the crown. The compound Ra-Horakhty — 'Rꜥ, Horus of the Horizon' — folded the royal sky-falcon into the sun. Greeks and Romans read him through Helios: Herodotus already treats the phoenix's visit to Heliopolis as a solar event, and Plutarch retells Rꜥ's wanderings as Greek myth in Egyptian dress. The most radical reform was also solar: Akhenaten's Aten cult of the fourteenth century BCE — one disk, no image — was a revolution carried out entirely in Rꜥ's theological vocabulary, and the swiftness of its erasure shows how tightly solar doctrine bound the state. Through it all the name held: five thousand years of theology circle the same two consonants, r and ꜥ.
lore.culturalLegacy: Rꜥ never ceased shining on the world's capitals. Rome took his obelisks — Augustus set one up in the Circus Maximus, and its red-granite siblings from Luxor now stand in London and on the Place de la Concorde, re-erected as trophies of Egyptomania rather than of the sun. The pyramid silhouette and the solar disk became the universal shorthand for Egypt itself, deployed from Masonic iconography to Hollywood; modern Egyptology restored his theology from texts and tombs, while new religious movements claimed him as ancestor of solar monotheism and films cast 'Ra' as everything from starship tyrant to enlightened lawgiver. The common thread is appropriation: every age has repolished the sun's name for its own mirror.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Egypt wrote Rꜥ without vowels — rꜥ, two consonants and the deep ayin — and asked the reader to supply the breath. That is the god in miniature: a skeleton of sound carried five millennia by faith, art and calendar. His myth encodes a complete philosophy of rule: light is a voyage, rule is a voyage, night is the price of day, and chaos is defeated nightly, not once — a theology without final victory, only an endless, disciplined morning. In that rhythm lies Egypt's deepest insight: order is not the absence of struggle but its daily success.

To restore the name as Rꜥ, ayin and all, is to refuse the museum's silence: the sun still rises, and the two-consonant name still fits it.

lore.archaeology: Solar cult is visible in the pyramid complexes of the Old Kingdom, the solar temple of Nyuserre at Abu Ghurab, and the great temples of Heliopolis, Karnak and Abu Simbel — whose facade colossi face the sun's rays at the equinoxes. The colossal obelisks of Heliopolis and Luxor, single shafts of Aswan granite, stood before the sun's temples; pairs from Luxor now stand in London and Paris. The Amarna boundary stelae and the Great Hymn to the Aten preserve Akhenaten's solar theology, and tomb paintings from the Valley of the Kings show Ra in his day- and night-barks, surrounded by protective deities.
